output.summary: KEP-1513 proposed a generic Certificates API (CertificateSigningRequest resource) so clients can request x509 certificates from a CA through an approver/signer workflow. The KEP's status is implemented, stage stable, and the sources say it went stable in 1.19.
output.rationale: The API gives Kubernetes clients a programmatic way to obtain x509 certificates, originally to support Kubelet TLS Bootstrap and later out-of-core PKI needs. The design separates approval (authentication and authorization of a CSR) from signing (constructing the certificate), with both interacting through the Kubernetes resource model. A kikisdeliveryservice comment says the KEP "went stable" in 1.19, and the sources describe the work as completed in that release cycle.

alternatives.option: Build specialized certificate issuance (e.g. LetsEncrypt) directly into Kubernetes
alternatives.why_not: Listed as a non-goal: "Build in support for specialized certificate issuance (e.g. [LetsEncrypt](https://letsencrypt.org/))."

alternatives.option: Use a built-in signer such as kubernetes.io/legacy-unknown for user applications
alternatives.why_not: Maintainer guidance says legacy-unknown is only supported via the v1beta1 API, and that new signers should be defined as named signerNames building on this API, e.g. spiffe.io/... or kubernetes.io/... proposals.

alternatives.option: Back-fill token/duration hint honoring into existing kubernetes signer definitions
alternatives.why_not: Maintainer said that since the field is an addition, existing implementations would not honor it, so in-tree signers would honor it only from a stated version forward (rcomment:637435291, PR #2759, not merged as part of this KEP).

evidence.quote: The Certificates API enables automation of x509 credential provisioning by providing a programmatic interface for clients of the Kubernetes API to request and obtain x509 certificates from a Certificate Authority (CA).
Non-Goals - Build in support for specialized certificate issuance (e.g. LetsEncrypt).

The API explicitly allows requesting a named signer in a CertificateSigningRequest, so that other signers can make use of it.
